name: c-split-century-bench
prompt: A tall vertical hand-inked illustration torn across its middle: a ragged horizontal rip with pale fibrous paper edges and a narrow strip of plain cream backing showing through the gap, kept empty for a caption. Upper piece, the year 1919: a wrought-iron park bench with scrolled armrests and wooden slats, drawn in warm brown sepia ink on rough, slightly yellowed laid paper, gravel underfoot, a gas lamp and a bare plane tree behind, a horse-drawn cab sketched faintly far down the path. Only one person is on that bench, at its right end: a stout, pear-shaped gentleman with grey mutton-chop whiskers, a monocle on a black ribbon, a tall silk hat tipped down over his right brow, a fur-collared overcoat, striped trousers and white spats, legs crossed ankle over knee, his right arm slung along the backrest and a fat cigar in his left hand, chin raised with a bored, satisfied smirk. Lower piece, today: the identical bench from the identical viewpoint, inked with the same nib in cooler blue-black on bright white paper, now beside a council wheelie bin and a slim LED lamp post with a flat panel head, a tarmac path, and a commuter hurrying past in a puffer jacket, head bowed, face lit pale by a phone screen. At that bench's right end sits the very same gentleman, line for line unchanged: same whiskers, monocle, coat, spats, crossed legs, arm on the backrest, cigar, smirk, and silk hat tilted at exactly the same angle. Camera straight on at seated eye level, the bench centred and the same size in both pieces so its uprights line up across the tear. One low late-afternoon sun from the left lights both eras alike, throwing long shadows to the right beneath the bench, built from dense cross-hatching and fine parallel strokes, editorial newspaper cartoon draughtsmanship of the 1910s, confident wiry outlines, generous white paper. Purely pictorial: no lettering, captions, labels or marks of any kind are drawn. Thanks.
